source.title: A Proposal for Scaling the Scaling Laws
source.authors: Wout Schellaert; Ronan Hamon; Fernando Martínez-Plumed; J. Hernández-Orallo

record.file_problem: none; the full paper is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper conceptually tests aggregate versus instance-level extrapolation in a synthetic scaling example, but does not reproduce language-model pretraining-loss measurements.
record.gate_note: The only relevant original result is a synthetic benchmark example: a power law is fit to aggregate scores and compared with an instance-level MLP predictor. The paper does not measure held-out language-model loss, parameter/token/compute scaling, compute-optimal allocation, or actual downstream model performance. Cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a position paper. Its only result is a synthetic example in which the authors design the scores to depend on an abstract system feature. No real language model, pretraining loss or real downstream benchmark is measured, so nothing in it can show whether any version holds. The example illustrates the argument that aggregate scores can hide subgroup scaling; it does not test it. The argument is aimed at V6/V7-type predictability, but rests on constructed data and cited work, so it is treated as discussion.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue that summarising both systems and task performance hurts the predictive accuracy and generalisation of scaling analysis. They propose instance-level evaluation records plus assessor models to predict scores for hypothetical scaled-up systems. They support this only with an illustrative synthetic example.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a synthetic benchmark and an aggregate-score power-law illustration, then proposes an instance-level MLP-style predictor; it does not measure language-model pretraining loss or sweep parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The synthetic example varies task-instance subpopulation; the paper describes different score trends for the two subpopulations, but reports no numerical comparison by subgroup.

fits_no_version.finding: In a constructed example with two subpopulations, a power law fitted to mean scores of the 7 smallest synthetic systems misses the 3 largest. An instance-level MLP predictor tracks them. The scores are synthetic by design and no errors are reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aggregate-score scaling fits can mispredict when benchmark subgroups scale differently; instance-level assessor models may extrapolate better (illustrative, synthetic only).

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the First edition of the Workshop on the Scaling Behavior of Large Language Models (SCALELLM), Association for Computational Linguistics, 2024.
record.problems: The extrapolation demonstration is synthetic; it reports no numerical prediction errors or uncertainty, and uses only ten hypothetical systems and a simple two-subpopulation dataset. It does not validate results on actual language models or pretraining loss.

untested.parts: No other modality or training regime.
No real downstream task or real model; only synthetic, designed scores.
No fitting-choice comparison on real data. Non-universality of laws is asserted only via citations.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled this 'tests/T2' with V6 verdicts. Those are dropped because the data are synthetic and constructed to show the authors' point, so they cannot bear on whether real downstream performance scales predictably. R2 is the authors' own method compared against a baseline.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss across parameters, tokens, and compute is not measured.
No power-law extrapolation of language-model loss to runs orders of magnitude larger is tested.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and tokens is tested.
Architecture effects at fixed parameter count are not tested.
No other modality or training regime is tested.
Tested only with a synthetic benchmark-score example, not actual downstream tasks or language models; no relationship to pretraining loss is tested.
The paper does not test how fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation vary with setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: ten synthetic AI systems
rows.size_stated: Synthetic system feature values 10–100; the feature is an abstract scalable feature, with parameter count given as an example.
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to mean scores from the smallest seven systems and use it to predict the last three systems.

conditions.value: 1000 synthetic instances divided into two subpopulations

rows.measure: Power-law extrapolation of aggregate mean benchmark scores to held-out systems
rows.note: The paper states that aggregate measures cannot model the illustrated behavior accurately; the figure shows the fitted power law, but no numerical prediction errors are reported.
rows.check: Scores are synthetic and built by design. A power law fitted to designed means says nothing about real downstream predictability (V6). No numbers are reported; the figure is only an illustration.

rows.subject: ten synthetic AI systems
rows.size_stated: Synthetic system feature values 10–100; the feature is an abstract scalable feature, with parameter count given as an example.
rows.operation_detail: Train a default-parameter scikit-learn MLPRegressor on instance-level evaluation records, then aggregate its score predictions for larger systems.

conditions.value: 1000 synthetic instances divided into two subpopulations

rows.measure: Extrapolated instance-level scores, aggregated into system predictions
rows.baseline: Power-law fit to aggregate mean scores
rows.note: The text says the instance-based approach can correctly extrapolate to larger systems; the plotted predictions have no reported numerical error.
rows.check: This compares the study's own proposed method (an instance-level MLP) with an aggregate power law on synthetic data. That is a method comparison, not a measurement of the claim, so it should not be a claim row. No error numbers are reported.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
